name: Karosta Prison
label: Karosta Prison
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Zemgales iela' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Zemgales iela' (way/32122640): point nearest the subject (855 m long).
pin_note: Position from OSM W88674462 (Karosta Prison): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Former military prison now a museum and hostel.

text.description:
Karosta Prison is the red-brick prison building in Liepāja's Karosta area, with a watchtower close to the entrance. In the yard there are some striking outdoor exhibits: a military truck, a field kitchen and an amphibious vehicle. The yard is the one place where the building itself fills the frame, so it is the best choice for a classic picture of the prison.

It does not show the prison. Streets nearby, such as Zemgales iela, are a suggestion for a different kind of photo: weathered brick and Soviet-era buildings, many of them abandoned, which make moody, textured street pictures. Treat this area as a quieter extra stop, then walk over to the prison for the main shot.

At the prison, the red brick, the tower and the vehicles give you plenty to work with. Start wide to take in the building, then move closer for details such as brick texture, the tower or one of the vehicles. Photography is generally allowed in public areas, but check with staff about any restrictions, and confirm the yard is open to visitors on the day.
text.geographic_location: Karosta Prison is in Karosta, a district of Liepāja.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed for this spot, so plan the visit on foot. The route is through the streets, so keep an eye on the map as you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use 2x or the telephoto to pick out details such as brickwork or peeling surfaces. At the prison, the ultra-wide helps if you are close to the building and want the tower in the frame too.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Zemgales iela (walk through the streets near the prison, reached on foot). Abandoned, weathered brick and Soviet-era buildings in the street, a quieter alternative to the prison's own frontage; these are not views of the prison itself. For the prison itself, go to the yard of Karostas cietums, where you can frame the red-brick building and the watchtower near the entrance, with the truck, field kitchen and amphibious vehicle in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: On the street, use the lines of the buildings as leading lines and turn on gridlines to keep the verticals straight. In the prison yard, put one of the vehicles in the foreground and the brick building and tower behind it, so the picture has depth.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the red brick keeps its colour and the sky does not wash out. Keep gridlines on to avoid leaning walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is best for the street and the yard. Soft, even light, such as on a bright overcast day, shows the brick texture without harsh shadows.

text.access_note: Zemgales iela is a public street, but the prison and its yard may be ticketed or have restricted areas, so check the official site before you go.

name: Karosta
label: Karosta
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sv. Nikolaja Jūras katedrāle' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Svētā Nikolaja pareizticīgo Jūras katedrāle' (pois); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Former Russian military port district with historic buildings.

text.description:
Karosta is a former naval base on the northern edge of Liepāja, and it is unlike the rest of the city. The base was built between 1890 and 1906 for Tsar Alexander III. Later it became a closed Soviet military town, and at its busiest more than 20,000 people lived here. The Soviet forces left in 1994, and much of the area was left to decay. Today it draws visitors and artists with its fortress ruins, old admirals' houses and rows of block housing.

The best single photo here is of the Orthodox naval cathedral, St Nicholas (Sv. Nikolaja Jūras katedrāle). Its golden onion domes and decorated facade stand out against the plain concrete apartment blocks around it. That contrast is the picture: ornate and gilded in the foreground, grey and plain behind. It also tells you something about the district's history in a single frame.

On a phone, keep it simple. Stand in front of the main facade, on the Studentu rotas iela 7 side, and decide whether you want the whole building or just the domes. Include a little of the surrounding flats rather than cropping them out, because they give the scene its character. If you have time, two other spots in Karosta are worth a look: the canal at Oskara Kalpaka tilts, and the long North Pier, which has the ruined fortress behind it.
text.geographic_location: Karosta is a neighbourhood in the northern outskirts of Liepāja, on the Baltic coast, and covers about a third of the city's area. The cathedral stands among the district's blocks of flats.
text.directions_text: From central Liepāja, head north into Karosta and ask for Sv. Nikolaja Jūras katedrāle (the Orthodox naval cathedral). Get to the Studentu rotas iela 7 side, in front of the main facade. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade with some of the surrounding flats. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the building will not fit. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the domes alone against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the main facade, Studentu rotas iela 7 side). The golden onion domes and facade of the Orthodox naval cathedral, framed against the surrounding Soviet-era concrete apartment blocks. Nikolaja Jūras katedrāle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep the domes and facade as the main subject, and leave a strip of the plain blocks in the frame so the contrast shows. Turn on gridlines and keep the verticals straight so the building does not lean. If you are near the canal, Oskara Kalpaka tilts gives a waterside view of Karosta as an alternative. The North Pier gives a different shot, with the long breakwater and the ruined fortress behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the golden domes to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the gold keeps its detail and the sky does not turn white. Step back and use 2x or more rather than tilting the phone upwards, to avoid converging lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Clear daylight shows the gilding best. Early morning or late afternoon gives softer, warmer light on the domes.

text.access_note: The outside of the cathedral is open to photograph, but it is a place of worship and the interior is restricted, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Clear daylight shows gilded domes at their best.
Early morning or late afternoon gives softer, warmer light.
Standing back and using zoom rather than tilting the phone upwards reduces converging verticals.

name: St. Nicholas Naval Cathedral, Karosta
label: Naval Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Liepājas Svētā Nikolaja pareizticīgo Jūras katedrāle' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/87498075: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Nicholas's Orthodox Naval Cathedral' (69 m across).

text.description:
St. Nicholas Naval Cathedral stands in Karosta, the former naval district in the north of Liepāja. It was built in the style of 17th-century Russian churches, with a large central dome and four smaller domes around it. The designs were by Vasily Kosyakov, and the church was completed in 1903 to serve the Russian navy based here. Its later history was rough: it was used as a gymnasium and a cinema in Soviet times, and it was returned to the Orthodox Church after Latvian independence, with the first service held in December 1991.

For a phone photographer, the main appeal is the outside. The golden domes and ornate walls look very different from the plain grey apartment blocks nearby, and that contrast makes a strong picture. Stand in the grounds in front of the main facade, on the Studentu rotas iela 7 side, and you can fit the whole building and its domes in a single frame. Keep the walls upright by using the gridlines, and leave a little sky above the central dome so it does not look cut off.

The cathedral is an active place of worship and photography inside is not allowed, so plan to take your pictures from outside. Allow a few minutes to walk around the grounds, as the domes look different from each angle.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is in Karosta, the former naval district in the north of Liepāja. It stands among the apartment blocks of the area, with its main facade on the Studentu rotas iela 7 side.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot; head north from central Liepāja to Karosta and check the map for your route. The phone icon on the map marks the cathedral itself. Once you reach the building, walk into the grounds in front of the main facade and step back a little so the domes fit in your frame. Check the entrance on the map, as the address is given as Studentu rotas iela 7 in some places and Katedrāles iela 7 in others. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole cathedral. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the domes will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the golden domes and the decoration.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand in the grounds in front of the main facade on the Studentu rotas iela 7 side, a little way back from the building, so the domes fit in the frame. From here you see the golden domes and ornate exterior set against the grey Soviet-era apartment blocks nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the verticals straight. Include a strip of the grey housing at the edge of the frame if you want to show the contrast with the gilded church. Then take a closer shot of the domes with the telephoto lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the golden domes to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the gilding does not turn white against a bright sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around sunrise and sunset, when the low golden-hour light suits the exterior.

text.access_note: The exterior and grounds can be reached on foot from the street, but this is an active place of worship and photography inside is prohibited, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements.

name: Great Amber Concert Hall
label: Great Amber
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).

notes: Modern amber-coloured glass concert hall by the seaside park.

text.description: The Great Amber Concert Hall (Lielais Dzintars in Latvian) is Liepāja's concert hall and arts centre, and it is easy to recognise. The building is a cone-shaped structure wrapped in a tilted glass facade, so the walls lean and catch the sky instead of standing straight. That makes it a rewarding subject for a phone, because the reflections change with the weather and the time of day. The Liepāja Symphony Orchestra is based here. In March 2016 the hall also hosted the 24th Liepaja International Stars Festival for the first time. You will not fit all of it in at the default lens (1x), so switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) and let the leaning glass fill the frame. Use the gridlines to keep the edges tidy, and expect the lines to tilt a little because you are shooting up at the building. If you want a calmer picture, step back a few paces, or use 2x or more to pick out a section of glass and its reflections. Check the screen for your own reflection in the glass before you press the shutter.
text.geographic_location: The hall is in Liepāja, Latvia. Look at the hall on the map to see exactly which streets and open spaces surround it.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot; use the map to find your way to the hall. The phone icon on the map is about 15 m north of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the cone and the tilted glass in one frame. Then try the default lens (1x) for a tighter view, and 2x or more for details of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 15 m north of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up one vertical edge of the glass with a grid line. Tilt the phone slightly upward and accept that the walls will lean, because it suits this building. For a second picture, hold at 2x or 3x and fill the frame with the reflections in the glass, with no ground in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright part of the glass to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky reflections keep their detail. Take a few shots at slightly different angles, since glare changes as you move.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try it on a bright day with some cloud, when the glass shows sky and cloud patterns without harsh glare. If you are there after dark and the building is lit, use night mode and hold the phone steady against something firm.

text.access_note: The outside of the building can be photographed from the surrounding area, but for events, interiors or anything inside, check the official site before you go.

name: Holy Trinity Cathedral, Liepāja
label: Holy Trinity Cathedral
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/121221735: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Holy Trinity Cathedral' (73 m across).
notes: Baroque Lutheran cathedral with one of the world's largest mechanical organs.

text.description:
Holy Trinity Cathedral is a Lutheran church in Liepāja and the seat of the city's bishop. The city council decided to build it in 1742 for the German community. It was designed by the Königsberg architect Johann Christoph Dorn and consecrated on 5 December 1758. The architecture is late Baroque with classical touches, and the tower was raised to almost 55 metres in 1865–1866. That height makes it a rewarding subject to photograph.

Inside, the Rococo carving and gilding are the main draw. The church is also known for its organ, built by Henrich Andreas Contius in 1779. It has 131 stops and over 7000 pipes, and it was the largest mechanical organ in the world until 1968.

For a phone photo, the best shot is a steady view of the whole building with the tower rising behind the main body of the church. Keep the phone upright and level so the tower does not lean. If you go closer, switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) for the façade, or use the zoom for the clock and the upper tower. The cathedral also hosts concerts and exhibitions, so you may get a chance to see the inside too.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is in Liepāja, Latvia.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed nearby, so from central Liepāja make your way on foot or by whatever local transport you prefer, and head for Holy Trinity Cathedral (Liepājas Svētās Trīsvienības katedrāle). From there it is about 2 minutes on foot to the cathedral itself. The phone icon on the map is about 110 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full building and tower. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you move closer, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clock and tower top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 110 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. This distance lets you fit the whole tower in the frame with room around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it stands straight. Leave a little sky above the top, and include some ground at the bottom to show the scale of the building. If the whole church will not fit, take a second shot with the telephoto on the tower alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls and detail keep their colour. A Live Photo can be handy if people are passing in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a day with some light on the front of the church. Late afternoon or early evening may suit this side best, but check how the light falls when you arrive.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the street, but visiting inside, tours and the tower may have set times or tickets, so check the official site before you go.

name: Liepāja Theatre
label: Liepāja Theatre
camera_source: Commons cluster (1 photos), weak. Moved 27 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 190 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/235335196: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Liepājas teātris' (68 m across).
notes: The oldest professional theatre building in Latvia.

text.description:
Liepāja Theatre (Liepājas teātris) is the town's theatre, and it has been going since 1907, which makes it a good stop if you like a bit of history in your photos. A working theatre building gives you a strong, simple subject: a solid frontage, doorways and, if they are on show, signs or posters that say something about the town's cultural life. It is also a useful marker for the rest of your walk, so one good frame here helps tell the story of your day in Liepāja.

The building is best treated as a portrait of a single subject. Try to keep the whole frontage in the picture and give it a little space around the edges, so it does not look squeezed. Stand square on and switch on the gridlines, which helps keep the vertical lines of the walls straight. A slight step to one side, then a second shot at an angle, gives you a different feel with almost no effort.

If people are walking past, wait a moment and let one or two come into the frame. They show the scale of the building and make it feel lived in. Check the lens for fingerprints before you start, as a clean lens makes a visible difference to sharpness.

The theatre may be busier on performance evenings, which can be lovely for atmosphere but harder for a clean view. If you want to see inside, check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Liepāja Theatre (Liepājas teātris) is in Liepāja, Latvia.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops are listed for this spot. Use the map to head for the theatre. That is about 3 minutes on foot, so you can walk across for a closer look once you have your first shot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole frontage. From where you stand the theatre is some distance away, so try 2x or more on the telephoto lens to fill the frame without moving. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you walk right up to the building and cannot fit it in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Take one frame from there, then walk towards it if you want a closer view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the building with the vertical grid lines. Keep the whole front in view with a little space around it. Hold the phone level and do not tilt it upwards, or the walls will lean inwards. Take a second shot closer up, focused on the entrance. Include any signs or posters if they are there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the theatre to set focus, then slide the exposure slider down a touch if the sky is bright, so the building is not left in shadow. Take a few frames, as moving people and cars will change the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the whole frontage is easy to see. A bright overcast day also works well, as it gives even light with no harsh shadows. If you are in town for a performance, an evening visit adds atmosphere, and night mode can help if the building is lit.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street, but check the official site before you go for any access to the inside or to performances.
claims_not_in_sources: The theatre may be busier on performance evenings.
The theatre's frontage is visible from the street and can be photographed from outside.

name: Liepāja Lighthouse
label: Liepāja Lighthouse
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dienvidu mols' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Dienvidu mols' (way/185546725): point nearest the subject (700 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/904240834: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Liepājas bāka' (8 m across).
notes: Historic lighthouse on the Baltic coast.

text.description: Liepāja Lighthouse stands on the south side of the harbour, close to the entrance, so it is one of the first things you notice when you look across the port. The tower was built in 1868 from cast iron made by melting down ship wreckage. It has a few marks from its past. During the First World War the German light cruiser SMS Augsburg hit it with sixteen shells, and the dents can still be seen in the outer cladding. Some of the newer iron sheets carry the letters KOD, which stands for Liepāja. It photographs well because the slim tower is easy to pick out, and from the pier you can include water, quays and working harbour around it, which gives the picture a sense of place. Start with a wide shot of the whole scene, then step in closer for the tower on its own. If the iron looks dark against a bright sky, tap the tower to focus and pull the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Keep an eye on the weather out on the pier, as it can be breezy, and hold your phone with both hands. Check current access before you go, as the tower itself may not be open to visitors.
text.geographic_location: On the south bank of Liepāja's harbour, near the entrance, where the Baltic coast meets the port. The south pier, Dienvidu mols, runs out beside it.
text.directions_text: From there the lighthouse is to the south-east, about 440 m away. Use the map to follow the path between the two. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tower with the harbour around it. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the tower and its cladding from a distance, and ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the pier and port in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Dienvidu mols (base of the south breakwater, where the lighthouse stands). The lighthouse from the south side of the harbour, with the port and piers around it. The tower is to the south-east, so face that way.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the tower on one of the vertical lines, leaving some of the pier or water in the foreground. Keep the phone level so the tower does not lean. For a second picture, zoom in to 2x or more to fill the frame with the tower and the marks on its metal sheets.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright. If the wind makes the phone shake, hold it with both hands and take a few shots in a row.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear afternoon or early evening, when the light should fall on the side of the tower you can see. Avoid midday, when the sky is whitest. Look at the weather before you set out, as the pier is open to the wind.

text.access_note: The pier is an open outdoor walk, but the lighthouse tower may be closed to visitors, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: In the afternoon and early evening the sun is likely to light the side of the tower facing the stand-here point, because the tower lies to the south-east of it.
The pier can be windy.
The sky is usually whitest around midday.

name: Liepāja Museum
label: Liepāja Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kūrmājas prospekts' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Kūrmājas prospekts nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/447748102: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Liepājas muzejs' (114 m across).
notes: City history museum in a historic building near the old town.

text.description:
Liepāja Museum is the largest museum in the historical region of Courland, and it sits in an early 20th-century building on Kūrmājas prospekt. The street is a good place for a walk and for photographing historic architecture. The museum holds more than 100,000 items, though only about 1,500 are on show in the halls. Displays cover the history of Liepāja from its early days and the ethnography of South Kurzeme. There is also a special collection of tinware and an exhibition on the woodcarver Miķelis Pankoks. The museum also keeps the archive of Paul Max Bertschy, the city's former architect. It moved into this building in the mid-1930s, so older photos of the museum may show a different house.

For a phone photo, the building is the subject. Cross to the opposite side of the street, face the front facade at No. 16/18, and take a first shot of the whole frontage with some of the street around it. Then step to one side and shoot along the building, so the line of the facade leads the eye down the street. Finish with a closer shot of a doorway or window. Parked cars and passers-by may cross the frame, so wait a moment for a clear view. The museum is also a good rainy-day stop if you want to see inside; check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Liepāja on Kūrmājas prospekts, at No. 16/18, in a street known for its historic buildings.
text.directions_text: No tram or train stops are listed nearby, so come on foot or by taxi and ask for Kūrmājas prospekts 16/18. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and the whole facade will not fit. Use the default lens (1x) for a natural look, and the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as doorways, windows and decoration.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kūrmājas prospekts (opposite the museum's front facade at No. 16/18, shooting along the building). The museum's street facade and its early 20th-century building, with the surrounding Kūrmājas prospekt streetscape. For a second angle, walk a little along the pavement and shoot along the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the edges of the building so the walls do not lean. Keep the facade in the middle with a little pavement and sky around it. For a more dynamic image, shoot along the front of the building from a corner of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright and washing out the walls. Hold the phone level and keep your elbows tucked in. If the ultra-wide stretches the edges, move back or switch to the default lens (1x).
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight when the facade is evenly lit gives the clearest detail. Early morning or late afternoon usually means fewer people on the pavement.

text.access_note: The outside of the building can be photographed from the public street; for the exhibitions inside, check the official site before you go.

name: St. Joseph Cathedral, Liepāja
label: St. Joseph Cathedral
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/305592560: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Liepājas Svētā Jāzepa Romas katoļu katedrāle' (66 m across).
notes: Neo-Romanesque Catholic cathedral with twin towers.

text.description: St Joseph Cathedral is the Roman Catholic cathedral of Liepāja and the seat of the Diocese of Liepāja. It is built in the neo-Romanesque style, and its solid, heavy shapes make a strong subject for a phone photo. The story behind it is quite modest. Liepāja's first Catholic church was a small wooden one from 1508, dedicated to Saint Ann, and it was converted to Lutheran worship around 1560. Catholics then had to travel to Lithuania for baptism and the other sacraments. A small stone church of Saint Joseph followed in 1747, but it became too small as the city grew. The present church, designed by the architect Luis Melvil, was completed and consecrated in 1911. In 1937 Pope Pius XI created the Diocese of Liepāja, and the church became a cathedral. The phone icon on the map is about 45 m north-east of the subject. From there you can take in the whole cathedral without craning your neck. Then walk closer for detail shots of the entrance and the stonework. Keep the phone level so the walls stay straight, and switch on gridlines to help. If people are walking past, wait a moment for a clear gap rather than cropping them out afterwards. Be considerate if a service is under way.
text.geographic_location: In the city of Liepāja, Latvia.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The phone icon on the map is about 45 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) at the phone icon on the map to get the whole building in. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close to the walls and want everything in frame. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details higher up the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 45 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. From here the whole building fits in the picture. Move closer for detail shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a vertical edge of the building up with a grid line to keep the walls straight. Hold the phone level and avoid tilting it upwards, which makes the building lean. Leave a little space around the building rather than cutting it tightly. For a second picture, move in close and use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for a dramatic view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. If the light is poor, use night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light on a clear day usually shows stonework best. Overcast light is fine too, since it avoids harsh shadows.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, so check the official site or the cathedral's notices for visiting arrangements and dress expectations before you go inside.

name: Monument to the sailors and fishermen perished in the sea
label: Sailors Monument
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jūrmalas parks' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jūrmalas parks' (way/75376573): edge nearest the subject (1597 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1198048984: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Piemineklis bojā gājušajiem jūrniekiem un zvejniekiem' (10 m across).
notes: Seaside memorial on the Liepāja beach.

text.description:
This is a tall bronze figure of a woman, standing on a V-shaped pedestal in Liepāja's seaside park and looking out over the Baltic. The monument remembers sailors and fishermen lost at sea. It was designed by architect Gunārs Asaris and sculptor Alberts Terpilovskis and built in 1977. The pedestal is 11 metres high and covered in Saaremaa dolomite. Locals often call it "Crocodile" because the pedestal resembles Crocodile Gena from a Soviet cartoon. A memorial plate for American airmen shot down near Liepāja in 1950 was added to the pedestal in 2000.

It photographs well because the statue has room around it. Walk the short distance to the monument for a different picture. Standing close and looking up shows the woman against the sky, framed by the pedestal walls. The inner part of the pedestal is a popular place for photographs. The plaque is in English and Latvian, so a close-up of it makes a good second shot. The monument stands on a sand rampart by the sea, so expect a strong wind and little shelter.
text.geographic_location: The monument is in Liepāja's seaside park (Jūrmalas parks), on the Baltic shore at the end of Kūrmājas prospekts. The Kurhaus once stood here in the early 20th century.
text.directions_text: The monument is in the seaside park at the end of Kūrmājas prospekts. From there the monument is to the east, about 1 minute on foot. The park is also a stop on walks to the beaches. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wide view that shows the statue with the park and dune. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you go up close to the pedestal and look up. A telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) helps for the bronze figure's face and for the plaque.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Jūrmalas parks (seaside park area around the monument, at the end of Kūrmājas prospekts). The monument set against the seaside park greenery and the dune, with the woman's figure looking out over the Baltic. The monument is to the east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the monument on one of the vertical lines, leaving some greenery and sky around it. Keep your phone upright so the full height of the figure and pedestal fits. For a second shot, walk up to the monument and aim upwards from below, using the dolomite pedestal walls as a frame around the bronze woman. Another option is a close-up of the memorial plate.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the figure to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky does not wash out and the bronze keeps its detail. Hold the phone with both hands, as the wind can shake it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Afternoon or evening is a good choice for the view from where you stand, when the sun is behind you. Early in the day or on a quieter weekday gives you more chance of a shot without other visitors.

text.access_note: The monument is in an open seaside park; check the official site before you go if you want to be sure of any ticket or entry rules.

name: Liepāja Station
label: Liepāja Station
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Liepāja Station' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/7799314251: the OpenStreetMap point 'Liepāja'.
notes: Historic railway station of the city.

text.description: Liepāja Station is the city's railway station, on the Jelgava–Liepāja line. It was built in 1871 as the first station on the Libau–Romny Railway, Libau being the German name the city went by at the time. It suits a quick, relaxed photo stop. The best picture is the straight-on view from the front forecourt, where the main entrance and the whole facade sit in front of you. If the round fountain basin is still there, it makes a neat foreground to lead the eye towards the building. The roofs and buildings of the city on either side of the station give a sense of where it sits. The station yard looked different in earlier times, so it is worth comparing with what you see today. The layout may have changed, so look around when you arrive. Stand back far enough to fit the full width of the building in the frame, and keep the phone level so the walls don't lean. Check for people and vehicles coming and going, and wait a moment for a clear gap. A few steps left or right will change the angle and help you avoid cars or signs.
text.geographic_location: The station sits at the north end of Jaunliepāja, about 20 minutes' walk from Tram Bridge (Tramvaja tilts).
text.directions_text: No tram or rail stops are listed for this spot. From Tram Bridge (Tramvaja tilts), it is about 20 minutes on foot to the station. Walk to the front of the building, where the phone icon on the map marks the forecourt. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the forecourt is tight or you want to include the fountain and the buildings either side. Use 2x if you prefer to focus on the entrance and keep out cars and signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you look straight at the main facade across the forecourt, with the round fountain basin in the foreground if it is still there, and the city's buildings on both sides.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the entrance up with the centre of the frame. Keep the phone upright and level so the building doesn't lean. Put the fountain basin low in the frame as a foreground and leave the sky above the roof. Then take a second shot from a few steps to one side for a different angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. With the ultra-wide, keep the building away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the facade is evenly lit and the forecourt is fairly quiet. Look at the building on the day and move around until the light isn't hitting the lens directly.

text.access_note: Check the station's current layout on the spot before you shoot.
